job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm doing a master's in structural engineering in Sheffield, where I also did my civil engineering degree. Mornings are lectures on steel connections, afternoons are the library or the lab, and on Thursdays I help my tutor mark bridge-load reports. I did ten weeks last summer at a bridge inspection firm, mostly climbing around with a clipboard, and I loved it. I pay no rent worth mentioning because my parents backed me, so the main stress is making my thesis good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the lab I'd shrug and say hype comes and goes. I'd tell my dad, who's an electrician and a union rep, that it's the same story as every new gadget. Online I'd probably say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my field stays safe. Nobody signs off a bridge because a chatbot told them to, and a chartered engineer's stamp is a legal thing. I do worry a bit that I never touch these tools while classmates do, but I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to the three inspection and design firms I already know, and keep my savings where they are. I'd keep doing my calculations by hand first and only then check them in the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it feels fine, a bit boring even. I like boring when it comes to where my pay comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use these tools. What would make you try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably if my supervisor told me a client demanded it. I tried one once for a report summary and it invented a standard that doesn't exist, so I closed the tab. I'd need to see it get codes right for a whole year before I trusted it with a load calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if the plateau held?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Tobi, who does data entry for an insurer. Even a small amount of automation can take away his hours. I'd be the one lending him money, which I'm fine with, but it would bother me.

say: I'd say the hype will **fade** and the real work of building things carries on as always.
At family dinners I'd tell my dad it's **another gadget** and nothing to panic about.
think: I believe my **stamped engineering** work stays human because the law needs a named person to answer for it.
I quietly worry I'm **falling behind** classmates who already use these tools.
do: Finish the **master's thesis** on steel connections and apply to three firms I know.
Keep my **savings untouched** and carry on checking calculations by hand.
feel: I feel **steady** and a little bored, which suits me.
I feel a small **guilt** for not learning tools my classmates use.
S0.quote: Nobody signs off a bridge because a chatbot told them to, and a chartered engineer's stamp is a legal thing.
fieldNote: Zane is **secure** and knows it; his calm rests on the law needing a named engineer, not on trust in AI.
His refusal to use tools is principled and a little defensive.
His real concern is for his cousin Tobi, not himself.

steps.text: Finish the master's thesis on steel connections by June
Apply to three bridge and building firms I interned near

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift, but a managed one if governments and unions do their job. At the uni union I'd push for rules on how firms use these systems on public projects. To friends I'd say learn the basics, even though I can't say I've taken my own advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my calculation checks and drawing reviews are exactly the kind of thinking tasks that move to software. Junior roles are where firms save money, and I'm applying for a junior role. That makes me uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the department's module on automated design tools, which I've been dodging. I'd ask my dad to introduce me to his union's training officer, and I'd still apply to firms with strong engineers on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a tide coming in slowly. I'm not drowning, but I can feel it at my ankles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a firm that wants fewer juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the managing director that juniors become the seniors who sign the drawings in ten years. If nobody trains them, the firm has no one to sign anything. It's a self-defeating cut and I'd say so in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day is most at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checking part, where I compare a hand calculation to a spreadsheet. A tool does that in seconds. The site visits, where you stand under a bridge and look at rust, are far harder to replace.

say: I'd say change is real but **rules and unions** must decide how firms use it.
I'd tell friends to learn the **basics** of these tools, though I haven't yet.
think: The checking and review tasks I'd do as a **junior** are exactly what software takes first.
Firms cutting junior hiring now will have **no seniors** later, but that's no comfort today.
do: Sign up for the **automated design module** this term, even though I've avoided it.
Ask my dad to introduce me to his union's **training officer**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, like a slow tide rising at my ankles.
S1.quote: Juniors become the seniors who sign the drawings in ten years. If nobody trains them, the firm has no one to sign anything.
fieldNote: Zane shifts from **principle** to practical: he is willing to move, but only under pressure.
Strong union upbringing frames AI as a labour-relations question first.
He separates desk checking from site inspection and places his hope in site work.

steps.text: Take the automated design tools module at university this term
Ask dad's union for a free training session on AI at work
Apply to firms that still run graduate training schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is awful. I'd say publicly that governments need to freeze new deployments in public works until safety rules exist. I'd go on a union march if one were called, and I'd say it to my father's face that regulators were asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree loses most of its pricing power before I even use it. By 2028 I'm 26, with a master's that's worth a lot less, and I'd be competing with software for my first drawing job. The robots for site work come later, around 2031, and that's where I'd have to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the master's after this term if the job market looks hopeless, and go to a site apprenticeship with a contractor. I'd sell my second-hand car and keep my savings for my parents' bills. I'd also join the union as a student member the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel sick. I'd lie awake doing sums. I've done well, I did all the right things, and it still might not matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for it coming this fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies racing each other with no one making them slow down. I blame the politicians who took their donations too. Nobody voted for this speed, and that's what makes me angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Ada that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep her nursing degree, because patients will still need hands for a while. I'd tell her I'm scared and that we'd manage, because our parents have savings and we'd share. I wouldn't pretend to know more than she does.

say: I'd demand a **freeze** on new deployments in public works until safety rules exist.
I'd join a **union march** and tell my dad regulators were asleep.
think: My master's could lose most of its **worth** before I ever use it in a job.
The **site work** that robots reach last is where I'd have to go.
do: Stop the master's after the term and take a **site apprenticeship** with a contractor.
Join the union as a **student member** within the week.
feel: I feel **sick** and I lie awake doing sums.
I feel **angry** that nobody voted for this speed.
S2.quote: Nobody voted for this speed, and that's what makes me angry.
fieldNote: Zane's calm **breaks** fully; his anger goes to companies and politicians, not to the technology.
He is the only one here willing to drop the master's for site work.
Family safety net is real but he doesn't want to lean on it.

steps.text: Pause the master's after this term and look for a site apprenticeship
Join the engineers' union as a student member this month
Sell my second-hand car and keep the cash for family bills
Write to my local politician demanding rules on public-works AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to complain loudly and still do something about it. I'd tell the union I'm in that we need a training fund for graduates before 2031. I'd tell friends I'll still be an engineer in 2031, just maybe a different kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be nervous but not wrecked. I'd have finished the master's, worked three years, and gotten my chartered status started. By 2031 the thinking tasks go to AI, so I'd need to be the person who walks the site and signs the paper, before robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the first firm that offers a site-heavy role, and do my chartership exams as fast as I can. I'd also take a basic AI tools course, reluctantly, to show I can supervise one. And I'd save a fifth of whatever I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable but heavy. Like a deadline that's far enough away to plan for and close enough to ruin my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still refuse to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't let an AI do my safety checks unseen. I'd use it to draft a report but check every line myself. If a firm insisted I sign off work I couldn't verify, I'd quit that firm and look elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change if you had the full five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be more daring with my first job. I'd choose an inspection firm over a big design office. With five years I can afford to start somewhere unglamorous and learn site skills that stay valuable.

say: I'd tell my union we need a **graduate training fund** before 2031.
I'd tell friends I'll still be an **engineer** in 2031, just maybe a different kind.
think: Five years is enough to get **chartered** and be the person who signs the site paperwork.
The **thinking tasks** go first, so I must own site skills before robots arrive.
do: Finish the master's and take the first **site-heavy** role offered.
Sit **chartership exams** as quickly as I can and save a fifth of my pay.
feel: I feel **nervous** but not wrecked, like a deadline that's far enough to plan for.
S3.quote: I wouldn't let an AI do my safety checks unseen. I'd use it to draft a report but check every line myself.
fieldNote: With five years Zane turns **planning**-minded; chartered status is his protection.
He will use tools only to supervise them, never to replace his own checking.
He draws a firm ethical line on signing unverified work.

steps.text: Finish the master's and accept a site-heavy first role
Sit the chartered engineer exams within three years
Save a fifth of every pay cheque from the first month
Take a short course on supervising AI design tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say it's the best chance we get to do this properly. I'd push the union and the university to build retraining into every engineering degree. To friends I'd say use the decade, don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved. I'd be 34 by 2036, probably senior and chartered, with ten years of site judgement that's hard to copy. The robots reaching hands-on work around 2039 are a later problem for my career, though maybe not for my kids'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a normal graduate job, climb the ladder, and mentor juniors myself so the chain doesn't break. I'd learn the AI tools gradually, one project at a time, because I'd have the luxury of choosing. I'd buy a flat with my savings and a mortgage, since ten years gives time to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, nearly hopeful. There's a decade for rules to catch up with the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still make you worried here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether rules actually arrive. Ten years of drift is a decade the companies use to get ahead. I'd have to be active in my union or I'd be wasting my own safety margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your classmates who think this is all overblown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I say good, hope you're right, and use the time to learn site skills anyway. If they're right, I lost nothing. If they're wrong, they're ready. I just don't tell them I'd also be happy to be wrong.

say: I'd say a decade is the best chance to build **retraining** into every engineering degree.
I'd tell friends to **use the decade** and not waste it.
think: By 2036 I'd be **chartered** with ten years of site judgement that's hard to copy.
The real risk is **drift**, ten years of no rules while companies get ahead.
do: Take a normal **graduate job** and mentor juniors so the training chain doesn't break.
Learn the **AI tools** gradually, one project at a time.
feel: I feel **hopeful**, almost relaxed, because there is a decade for rules to catch up.
S4.quote: If they're right, I lost nothing. If they're wrong, they're ready. I just don't tell them I'd also be happy to be wrong.
fieldNote: Ten years returns Zane to his **comfort** zone: slow change, union pressure and mentoring.
He is prepared to learn tools only when the pace is his own.
His worry shifts from jobs to whether governments actually act.

steps.text: Join a graduate scheme and mentor the interns who follow
Learn one AI design tool per project over several years
Push the union to demand training funds for graduates

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because nobody gets time to adapt and the people with the least say pay first. What would help is a rule that firms must keep training juniors, and a public fund for people whose degrees lose value. I'd also want my parents' savings protected from a bad year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Yes, I wish you'd asked what I'm proudest of. It's passing my steel exam without help, and nobody, human or software, can take that off me.

headlineQuote: I've done well, I did all the right things, and it still might not matter.
portrait: Zane is 24, doing a master's in **structural engineering** in Sheffield with strong family backing and no debt.
He grew up around his father's **union** and sees AI as a question of rules and who gets to decide.
He never uses AI tools and trusts hand checks, which keeps him calm in slow scenarios.
In the two-year world his calm breaks and he would consider a **site apprenticeship** over finishing his degree.
With five or ten years he plans, mentors and pushes for **training funds** rather than panics.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries him most because no one has time to adapt and graduates pay first.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that firms must keep **training juniors**, plus a public fund for people whose degrees lose value.
